Update: Nominated for the Stream Awards! :)

I've been on some sort of espionage spree of games and it doesn't seem to be stopping. First off, this game needs way more attention than it's getting. It took me around 8 hours to complete and it's been fun the whole way through. I'll just go over some pros and cons so I don't start talking about my new obsession more than I already have.

Pros:
- Awesome art style
- Long story
- Extra additions that aren't necessary but make the game way more interesting
- Half realistic hacking terminal
- AMAZING parody software and puns throughout
- Isn't too easy

Cons:
- Not so great replay value
- No punishment for convicting the wrong person
- Can't reply to emails and such to progress your own characters personality
- Same-old-same-old way of hacking people throughout the game
- Less psychology and more downloading and uploading files
- The deep web is on the surface web? (would be able to instantly track their IP and location but then again there are so many other unrealistic things in the game I guess it's fine)
- Boring news articles
- Needs more dynamic audio like in another similar game called 'Orwell'
- Could be more of a choose your own adventure

Now there are more cons than pros I will admit that but they're small cons that are just me being picky.  I still highly recommend it.

UPDATE: Still 10/10. Love. This. Game.

review_text_raw:
A good game, but could use some polish to become a great one.

Let me start with a pro/con list so you don't have to sift through my personal thoughts in longform.

Pros:
-Doesn't hold your hand, feels 'authentic'. You feel like you're hacking, in some small way.
-Satisfying UI, easy to navigate without tutorial.
-Challenging without being mind-bendingly difficult or frustrating (usually).
-Interesting story with fun twists and turns and a lot of personal flourish to make it feel alive.
-Offers several solutions to almost every case, the result is up to what you turn in.
-Good music and ambient sound.
Cons:
-Bit of a buggy mess sometimes. Had to reset several cases when things stopped working, and had the entire game freeze at one point.
-Doesn't do much to make you feel "involved" in the story...you are a silent and non-engaging protagonist. Things happen to you and around you, you do not really interact except hacking.
-A few times, it suffers from "Figure out what the devs were thinking" syndrome.
-Lots of typos and a few places where things were not implemented but were left in the script for players to see

Mainlining is a good game with a lot of potential. I love the concept of an adventure game told through hacking and desktop UIs. But it really needs a good strong polish to truly be a satisfying experience. It's a short, light-hearted bit of fun, which I enjoyed! Don't expect a deep hacking experience like Uplink...this is primarily an adventure game. However, the narrative was too short and not engaging enough for me to really feel totally sucked in or invested....exciting things lose their emphasis because it's all told to you the same way with very little pause for breath or impact, or it happens "off screen".

However, I think this game is fun, interesting, unique and worth a play for sure. I found it easy to forgive its little hiccups and lack of polish because I was so charmed by Mainlining. If you enjoy feeling like a hacker, government intrigue, solving mysteries and adventure games, I think you will really find something to like here.

Not Quite What I Expected

While the game has a decent plot with a unique charm reminiscent of "Papers, Please," it wasn't exactly what I was hoping for. I came in expecting a game rooted in real hacking mechanisms and knowledge, but unfortunately, the hacking aspect feels overly simplified. Most of it boils down to basic commands like "ping" and "use this computer on this IP," which left me wanting more depth and realism. That said, the detective narrative is engaging, and the game's style does offer a distinctive appeal. It’s worth a try if you're more into the story than the technical side.

review_text_raw:
Mainlining is a cyberpunk-inspired investigative adventure that turns the ordinary process of browsing files, reading emails, and searching databases into a tense and immersive detective experience. Developed by Rebelephant and published by Merge Games, the game places players behind the screen of a government intelligence computer system where every clue, suspect, and secret must be uncovered through hacking, surveillance, and careful analysis of digital information. Instead of relying on action sequences or cinematic set pieces, Mainlining builds suspense entirely through deduction, atmosphere, and the unsettling realization that every citizen’s private life is only a few clicks away from exposure.

The game is set in a near-future Britain where privacy laws have collapsed following the introduction of the BLU Pill Act, legislation that grants intelligence agencies unrestricted access to personal digital information. Players take on the role of an operative working for MI7, a government surveillance division tasked with tracking cybercriminals after a major breach compromises national security. What initially appears to be a series of disconnected investigations slowly evolves into a larger conspiracy involving corruption, abuse of power, political manipulation, and the dangers of mass surveillance. The story feels particularly effective because its themes mirror real-world debates surrounding government monitoring and digital privacy, giving the experience a level of relevance that extends beyond simple science fiction.

One of Mainlining’s greatest achievements is its presentation. The entire game takes place inside a simulated retro computer operating system inspired by older versions of Windows desktops. Every action occurs through email clients, command prompts, browsers, folders, chat programs, and intelligence databases, creating the illusion that the player is genuinely operating inside a classified surveillance network. This design choice immediately establishes immersion because players interact with the world exactly the way an investigator would. The retro-inspired pixel art and low-tech interface also contribute heavily to the atmosphere, giving the game a gritty and believable cyberpunk identity without relying on flashy visuals.

Gameplay revolves around investigating suspects by hacking into personal computers and analyzing digital traces left behind in their online activity. Players search through conversations, photographs, browsing histories, financial records, and social media interactions in order to uncover evidence and identify criminal behavior. Unlike many detective games that heavily guide the player toward obvious solutions, Mainlining encourages independent thinking and observation. Important clues are often hidden within seemingly unimportant files or casual conversations, forcing players to pay close attention to details instead of simply following objective markers.

The command-line hacking mechanics are surprisingly immersive despite their simplicity. Players use text commands to access networks, trace IP addresses, and infiltrate systems, creating the feeling of performing real investigative work without becoming inaccessible to newcomers. The game succeeds because it understands how to make information itself feel rewarding. Discovering a hidden message, uncovering an encrypted file, or linking multiple suspects together creates genuine excitement because progress depends entirely on the player’s own deductions rather than scripted sequences.

What truly separates Mainlining from other hacking-themed games is the moral discomfort that develops over time. Although the player technically works for law enforcement, many of the investigative methods feel invasive and ethically questionable. Reading intimate personal conversations, examining private photographs, and monitoring every aspect of someone’s digital life creates a constant sense of unease. The game repeatedly raises questions about whether unrestricted surveillance can ever remain justified once governments gain the ability to observe every citizen without limitations. Even when tracking criminals, the player often feels disturbingly close to violating the boundaries of innocent people.

The investigations themselves remain varied enough to keep the campaign engaging. Cases involve cybercrime, hacking groups, drug operations, financial fraud, and organized conspiracies that slowly reveal deeper connections hidden beneath the surface. Players must carefully identify suspects, gather evidence, and determine physical locations before making arrests. Wrong accusations can result in failure, adding pressure to every investigation and encouraging players to double-check conclusions before acting. This structure creates a satisfying detective experience because success feels earned through careful reasoning rather than random guessing.

The writing throughout the game is consistently strong. Dialogue balances serious political themes with dry humor and believable character interactions that prevent the experience from becoming overly bleak. Emails, online chats, and casual conversations reveal small personality details that make suspects and supporting characters feel authentic despite the minimalist presentation. The game gradually builds a believable world where political fear, digital dependence, and government overreach have become deeply intertwined with everyday life.

The soundtrack complements the atmosphere exceptionally well. Electronic music and ambient background tracks create a constant feeling of tension and paranoia without overwhelming the quieter investigative moments. Combined with the glowing retro desktop aesthetic and endless streams of digital information, the audio design reinforces the sense that players are trapped inside a cold and impersonal surveillance system.

Despite its originality, Mainlining is not completely free from flaws. Some investigations can become repetitive because the gameplay loop often revolves around similar patterns of searching files and tracing connections. Certain clues are occasionally too obscure, leading to moments where progression slows due to unclear objectives. The command-line interface, while immersive, can also feel awkward at times because typing errors or unclear system responses occasionally interrupt the pacing. Players expecting action-heavy hacking gameplay may also find the experience too slow because most of the tension comes from reading, analyzing information, and making logical deductions rather than participating in high-energy sequences.

The visual presentation, while stylish, is intentionally minimalistic and may not appeal to everyone. Those expecting large cinematic environments or highly animated storytelling may initially find the desktop-only structure limiting. However, the simplicity ultimately becomes one of the game’s strengths because it keeps the player fully focused on the investigation itself rather than external distractions.

Although it lacks major production values or complex action mechanics, Mainlining stands out as one of the more memorable indie hacking adventures available. Its investigative gameplay, morally ambiguous storytelling, and immersive interface design create a unique experience that rewards patience, observation, and curiosity. Players interested in conspiracy thrillers, cybercrime investigations, and narrative-driven puzzle games will likely find themselves completely absorbed by its dark digital world.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw:
Mainlining is a nifty little adventure game with a hacking theme that, unlike other hacking games available on steam, eschews the nitty gritty of command-line interface wizardry in favor of telling a succint story well within its means.  That is to say, if you've avoided other hacking games because they emulate real-world operating systems all too closely, you can relax - Mainlining's CLI is quite simple and doesn't require any foreknowledge of how command-line operating systems work.

Instead of bringing the hardcore keyboard thunder, Mainlining opts for funtional aesthetics.  When you first start up the game, you'll be looking at a pixelated mock-up of a WinXP-like desktop.  Though typing away in the CLI is a big part of the game, you'll only ever need three or four commands, all of which are easy to remember.  The rest is as you would normally navigate a desktop OS these days - with a mouse.  Throughout the game, you will load applications onto your start bar, read files on your desktop notepad, and browse a well-realized fake web, all the while using information you find to remotely hack into other systems.  Throughout several cases, you will follow a bread-crumb trail that will eventually unravel to reveal a story.

That story being you work for MI7, a sister org to the famous MI5, only its main focus is online activity facilitating real-world crimes, and the backdrop of all this is a new act simply called the BLU Pill.  While it never gets into specifics, BLU Pill basically enables the gov't to break into systems legally in order to fight crime.  Naturally, this angers a few people and they organize themselves into a secret hacking group to counter MI7's efforts.  The game makes no hard stance on the politics of such a law, but throughout the game, you're never quite sure if you're the good guy or the bad guy.

In any case, this is all handled with beautiful pixel-style art from end-to-end, from presenting you nostalgic mock-ups of popular desktops (WinXP, iOS, etc) to a whole database full of pixel faces of the citizens of wherever you are.  In terms of aesthetics, Mainlining really reminded me of Digital A Love Story, and it unfolds in a very similar manner.  As you read chat logs and other random files you nab off unsuspecting systems, you'll learn about the inhabitants of this world and the characters found therein.  Moreover, there are live chat windows on your screen that dole out large portions of the story and all you ever have are names.  You're not told who's who, but it eventually all slots into place.

While I didn't encounter any glaring bugs, the game doesn't give you a lot of options to go off-script, nor does it make any effort throw any red herrings at you so unless you're really trying to find ways to break the game, you likely won't have a problem.  At all times, I was patienly waiting for the proverbial Other Shoe, but it never really came.  As each day/case passes, you'll be told what you need to find in order to proceed and any previously-learned knowledge usually doesn't work again, so going off the beaten path doesn't really present itself.  You either figure out what to do next or you don't.

That being said, I completed the game in about 2 hours or so and never even so much as wished for a hint.  All of the challenges in the game are easily met and good segments of the game are just waiting around for some things to happen.  I can't really describe more since that would spoil it, but for the most part, it plays a lot like the old standard of cutscene -> gameplay -> cutscene.

All in all, I found Mainlining to be an enjoyable experience and a perfect entry point into the genre since it really does a little of everything.  Outside of some proofreading mishaps, the game is solid.
